To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have identified the first two genes, RSP9 and RSP4A, which, when mutated, cause PCD with a specific defect in the structure and function of the cilia.

mutations in RSPH9, encoding a component of the axoneme radial spoke head, and RSPH 4A, encoding a radial spoke protein, cause PCD with defects of the central-pairs of the axonemes of respiratory-tract cilia and sperm flagella.

mutations in two new genes, RSP9 and RSP4A, cause primary ciliary dykinesia with radial spoke head defects, and that these genes are important in cilia motility but not in left-right axis specification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a new genetic cause of PCD and the identification of a conserved mechanism of ciliary function in a range of organisms, from algae to humans.
a new class of PCD genes encoding components of the radial spoke head, which are essential for normal movement of "9+2" cilia and flagellum.
the identification and characterization of a novel PCD locus and the identification of two novel disease-causing genes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mutations identified in RSPH9 or RSPH4 cause a primary ciliary dyskinetic phenotype in humans and zebrafish.
the two RSPH genes identified here are the first genes to be associated with a central-pair defect in humans.
mutations in RSPH4 and RSPH9 cause PCD with central-micro tubular-pair abnormalities and that RSPH9 has an important function in ciliary movement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RSPH9 (6p21.2) and RSPH 4A (6q22.2) genes encode components of the axonal radial spoke head, and that mutations in these genes cause PCD with central-micro-tubular-pair defects.
mutations in RSPH9 or RSPH4 cause a subset of PCD patients with defects in radial spoke head proteins, and this is associated with central-pair abnormalities in the cilia.
RSPH9 (and RSPH4a) mutations result in a central-pair defect in motile cilia, but that these genes are not essential for normal left-right axis determination.
The main takeaway from our work is that

mutations in the genes encoding the RSPH4 and RSPH9 proteins, components of the radial spokes, are a common cause of central microtubule-pair abnormalities in PCD patients and that this phenotype is associated with a normal situs.
the radial spoke is an important component of the axoneme and that mutations of RSP genes can result in PCD.
RSPH9 (6p21.2-p21.1) and RSPH9A (6q22.3-q22.1) are the first identified genes encoding proteins of the radial spoke head to be associated with primary ciliary dysgenesis in humans.
